KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...

This evening, a dry backdoor cold front will move south from Canada. 
A stray shower can not be ruled out north of the mountains. 
Temperatures look to cool drastically after the frontal passage. For 
instance, in Kennebec county, temperatures should be in the upper 
60s currently. By tomorrow morning, temperatures will be in the 
upper 30s, with below freezing temperatures likely north of the 
mountains, and temperatures in the 40s along the coast and southern 
New Hampshire.

High pressure over New Brunswick will allow for light 
northeasterly winds through the day Tuesday, and should largely 
prevent temperatures from warming up through the day. This is 
meteorological phenomena called a cold air dam. For the 
population corridor, this likely will not pose any issues, as 
the cold temperatures will likely stay above freezing. Perhaps 
more concerning is how temperatures pan out across north-central
Maine and how long the cold air dam hangs on to below-freezing 
or near freezing temperatures across northwestern Maine.
 
Low pressure will move in Tuesday morning, with rain across most 
locations and freezing rain expected in elevations above 3000ft. For 
the frozen side of the storm, model guidance today has had a desire 
to bring more wintry precipitation into North-central Maine. 
From pattern recognition this makes sense given the guidance is 
almost always too warm during cold air damming. However, I don't
quite see this as translating to more snow, rather longer 
durations of mixed- precipitation: snow, sleet and freezing 
rain. If it does snow, A thick isothermic layer in the low-
levels should keep SLRs very low, and generally make it very 
difficult for any periods of all-snow.

By Tuesday night, high pressure over New Brunswick will continue to 
drift eastward. This will in turn, disrupt the consistent 
northeasterly winds that form and maintain the cold air dam. Without 
these northeasterly winds, warm air aloft is much more likely to mix 
down to the surface and will result in all locations in western 
Maine changing over to rain late in the evening. By this time most 
of the storm is over, and will depart the region overnight. Skies 
may even clear out a little by Wednesday morning.

For wintry accumulations, we're not expecting much. The low SLRs and 
an eventual changeover to ice and then plain rain should prevent 
snow from accumulating in this area, but just enough snow and sleet 
to form a coating to an inch is certainly possible up by Jackman or 
Moosehead Lake. However, even a trace of icing can make roads 
slippery so drivers in this part of the state should heed caution.

For rainfall amounts, the bulk of the precipitation is likely 
to fall across northern NH and Maine, with at over an inch 
likely in the northern half of NH and locations north of 
Portland. Southern NH and York county are most likely looking at
less, likely closer to a half an inch.

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...

The low gradually moves away during the daytime on Wednesday. 
Scattered showers likely linger across the higher terrain much 
of the day, while areas downwind of the mountains gradually dry 
out through the day. Temperatures warm once winds shift to 
westerly behind the system, which will take until late in the 
day for areas further east. Southern New Hampshire stands the 
best chance to see temperatures jump into the low to mid 70s in 
the afternoon, but areas further north and east will be pressed 
for time before the sunset to actually realize the warmer 
temperatures forecast by the NBM.

Relatively cooler and drier air settles in for Thursday as high
pressure builds across New England. Conditions look seasonable,
with highs ranging from the upper 40s across the north, to low 
60s along the coast.

KEY MESSAGE 3 DESCRIPTION...

By Friday, low pressure rides eastward into New England. The 
low deepens as it passes through, and becomes a pretty strong 
coastal storm as it moves through the Canadian Maritimes. 
Another round of beneficial rain looks likely during the Friday 
to Friday Night timeframe, with generally a half inch to an inch
of QPF.

As the low deepens while moving through the Canadian Maritimes,
a strong northwesterly flow develops across New England. 
Currently, a small area of modified Arctic air looks to be 
directed into New England this weekend. There remains the chance
that this airmass misses us to the east. However, at this time 
a cold airmass for mid October looks likely for the weekend, 
along with gusty winds. Highs in the 30s and 40s look likely for
Saturday, along with mountain snow showers. Lows likely dip 
below freezing all the way to the coastline in most areas, with 
widespread lows in the 20s. Temperatures look similarly chilly 
with less wind on Sunday, before temps begin to rebound early 
next week.
